before.content_html:
What Is Production?

Production is how a business turns raw materials, time and effort into something a customer will pay for. The method a business picks shapes its costs, its speed and the kind of products it can offer. A bespoke furniture maker in Yorkshire and Nissan’s Sunderland car plant both ‘make things’ — but their production methods could hardly be more different.

For this unit, you need to know three methods — job, flow and lean production — plus the idea of just in time (JIT) as a way of making production more efficient. Each method suits a different kind of business, and the wrong choice can sink profits.

Key Fact

Job production makes one-off, customised items. Flow production makes huge volumes of identical items on a continuous line. Lean production is a mindset applied on top — cutting waste to squeeze more output from the same inputs.

Job Production

Job production means making one product at a time, usually to a customer’s exact order. A bespoke furniture maker building a dining table for a specific customer, a wedding photographer, a hairdresser or a small sign-writing workshop all use job production. Each ‘job’ is different.

Because every item is unique, prices are usually high and workers need broad skills. Quality can be outstanding — customers pay a premium for something built just for them. The downside is slow output. You cannot make a thousand bespoke wardrobes in a day, no matter how hard you try.

Job production works when the customer wants something personal, when volumes are low, or when the product is complex and skilled — think bespoke tailoring on Savile Row, handmade guitars, a architect-designed extension or a one-off cake from a local baker. The higher unit price covers the slower speed and the skilled labour. It is the wrong choice for a product where buyers care about price, not personalisation — you would not use job production to make tins of baked beans.

Flow Production

Flow production moves the product continuously along an assembly line. Each worker or machine does one specific task, over and over, before passing the part on. Nissan’s Sunderland plant, Heinz’s bean-canning lines and Cadbury’s chocolate factories all run flow production.

Flow production thrives on scale. By making huge volumes of an identical product, economies of scale pull the average cost of each unit down. The trade-off: it only works for products where demand is huge and standardised. Breakdowns on the line are expensive because the whole factory grinds to a halt. And workers doing the same bolt-tightening task all shift can become bored, which hurts quality and retention.

Key Fact

Flow production produces at a low cost per unit but has a very high set-up cost. The Nissan Sunderland plant produced its ten-millionth car in 2019 — no job-production workshop could approach that scale.

Lean Production

Lean production is not a separate method so much as a mindset layered on top of job or flow production. Developed by Toyota in Japan, it attacks waste at every stage — waste of time, materials, space, movement and stock. Less waste means lower costs and faster delivery without losing quality.

Toyota’s Derbyshire plant at Burnaston was built around lean thinking. Workers can stop the line if they spot a defect, which prevents faulty cars travelling further down the process. Tools and parts are placed exactly where workers need them so no time is wasted fetching. Stock is kept to the absolute minimum.

Just In Time (JIT)

Just in time (JIT) is the best-known lean technique. Suppliers deliver parts directly to the assembly line moments before they are needed — not days in advance. Nissan Sunderland uses JIT: seats, dashboards and glass are delivered in the exact sequence the cars need them, hour by hour.

The benefits are huge. The business needs far less warehouse space, ties up less cash in stock, and damaged or obsolete parts almost disappear. But JIT is fragile. A strike at a supplier, a ferry delay or a snowstorm can stop production within hours because there is no buffer stock to fall back on. Many UK manufacturers had their JIT supply chains tested after Brexit border delays and during the 2021 semiconductor shortage.

Other lean techniques include kaizen (continuous small improvements suggested by shop-floor workers), 5S (sort, set, shine, standardise, sustain — a workplace-tidiness method that saves time), and cell production (grouping workers into small teams that finish a whole section rather than one repeated task). Each one chases the same goal: cut waste, lift quality, speed up output.

Lean is not only for factories. Pret A Manger uses lean ideas in its sandwich-making — ingredients are prepared each morning to forecast demand, and anything unsold by the end of the day is given to charity rather than warehoused. The waste-cutting principle is the same.

Choosing a Method

There is no ‘best’ production method — only the best fit for the business. A start-up making bespoke cakes cannot afford flow production’s set-up costs and does not need its scale. A global crisp manufacturer cannot meet demand with job production. The decision turns on volume, the customer’s willingness to pay for customisation, the skills of the workforce and how much capital the business can invest up front.
before.exam_tip_html: For a 6-mark Analyse question you can now pull on more than one factor, but markers still reward a developed chain of reasoning: ‘because… which means… which leads to…’ beats a bullet list every time. For a 9-mark Justify, weigh up both options and commit to one, using case-study detail. Never describe job, flow and lean in the abstract — always apply them to the specific business in the question.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the best definition of flow production?
A) Making one item at a time for a specific customer
B) Making large volumes of identical items on a continuous line
C) Making small batches then switching machines for the next batch
D) Making items only once a customer order arrives
practice_questions.marks: B) Making large volumes of identical items on a continuous line [1 mark]

Mastering (2): A stock-management method where materials and parts are delivered from suppliers exactly when they are needed for production, so almost no stock is held on site.
Secure (1): A method of receiving stock only when it is needed / holding very little stock.
Emerging (0): Vague or incorrect — e.g. ‘when things arrive on time’.

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage for a small bespoke furniture maker of using job production rather than flow production.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): A clear advantage with a developed chain of reasoning — e.g. Job production lets the maker customise every piece to the customer’s measurements and taste (1), which means the business can charge a premium price because each item feels unique (2), boosting profit margins even though output is low (3).
Secure (2): A clear advantage with some development but the reasoning stops short.
Developing (1): A valid advantage identified but not explained.
Emerging (0): No valid advantage or confuses with flow production.

practice_questions.text: A bakery uses flow production. Fixed costs per week are £4,800 and variable costs are £0.40 per loaf. The bakery produces 12,000 loaves per week. Calculate the total cost per loaf.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): Fixed cost per loaf = 4,800 ÷ 12,000 = £0.40 (1). Total cost per loaf = 0.40 + 0.40 = £0.80 (2). Correct answer with units and working shown (3).
Secure (2): Correct method shown but a slip in the arithmetic or missing units.
Developing (1): One correct step (e.g. calculates fixed cost per loaf) but fails to add variable cost.
Emerging (0): No valid method. Method marks are awarded even if the final figure is wrong, so working must be shown.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on Nissan’s Sunderland car plant of using just-in-time (JIT) stock management.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): A developed chain of reasoning, applied to Nissan, drawing on more than one factor. E.g. JIT means parts arrive at the line hour by hour, so Nissan needs far less warehouse space and ties up less cash in stock, freeing capital for investment in the plant. However, the plant becomes vulnerable — a Channel ferry delay or supplier strike could halt production within hours because no buffer stock exists. The net effect is lower running costs in normal conditions but much higher risk when supply chains are disrupted, as seen during recent semiconductor shortages.
Secure (3–4): Clear analysis of at least one impact with some development, applied to Nissan.
Developing (1–2): Identifies effects but reasoning is limited or not applied to the context.
Emerging (0): No valid impact or purely generic points.

practice_questions.text: Anya owns a growing cake business that currently makes one bespoke cake at a time. She is deciding whether to stay with job production or move to a flow-production line making a standard range of three cakes. Justify which method she should choose.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9): A clear decision supported by two developed reasons, weighed against the alternative, with context applied throughout. E.g. Anya should stay with job production because customers pay premium prices for bespoke cakes — moving to flow would require heavy investment in machinery and kill her unique selling point. Flow production would cut unit costs but she would lose the customisation that brings customers in. Her best route is to keep job production while using some lean techniques to reduce waste.
Secure (5–7): A clear judgement with at least two reasons but uneven development, or limited weighing of the alternative.
Developing (3–4): Some reasons listed on both sides but no real judgement.
Emerging (1–2): Describes the methods without choosing or justifying.
Around four minutes of the answer should be spent on the evaluative judgement itself.

before.exam_tip_html: For a 9-mark Justify on stock management, do not just list JIT pros and JIC cons — commit to one strategy and weigh it against the alternative using the specific business in the case study. Examiners advise around four minutes on the evaluative judgement itself; a one-line conclusion is not enough. Remember that you will not be asked to draw or interpret stock control charts.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes just-in-case (JIC) stock management?
A) Ordering stock only after the customer has paid
B) Keeping spare buffer stock so demand can always be met
C) Sending stock back to the supplier each evening
D) Holding no stock at all
practice_questions.marks: B) Keeping spare buffer stock so demand can always be met [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two factors that affect a business’s choice of supplier.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (2): Any two from — price, quality, reliability (1 mark each, up to 2). Other accepted factors: location, delivery speed, ethical/environmental credentials, payment terms.
Secure (1): One correct factor identified.
Emerging (0): No valid factor, or vague terms like ‘good ones’.

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit to a UK supermarket chain of managing an effective supply chain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): A clear benefit with a developed ‘because’ chain — e.g. An effective supply chain means fresh produce moves from farm to shelf quickly (1), which reduces wastage from food spoilage (2), cutting costs and protecting profit margins while keeping shelves fully stocked for customers (3).
Secure (2): Benefit stated with some development.
Developing (1): Benefit identified without explanation.
Emerging (0): No valid benefit.

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer buys 8,000 components at £3.50 each. The supplier offers a 5% bulk discount if the order is placed in a single delivery. Calculate the cost saving the bulk discount provides.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): Original total cost = 8,000 × 3.50 = £28,000 (1). Discount = 28,000 × 0.05 = £1,400 (2). Saving = £1,400 with units shown (3).
Secure (2): Correct method but arithmetic slip or missing units.
Developing (1): Calculates one step only.
Emerging (0): No valid method. Method marks are awarded even if the final figure is wrong, so working must be shown.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a UK supermarket chain of switching from just-in-case (JIC) to just-in-time (JIT) stock management.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): A developed chain of reasoning drawing on multiple factors. E.g. Switching to JIT would free up warehouse space and reduce cash tied up in stock, giving the supermarket capital to invest in stores or digital systems. However, supermarkets depend on predictable shelf availability — if a haulage strike delays deliveries, whole ranges disappear within hours, pushing customers to competitors. The efficiency saving is real but so is the brand damage if shelves empty. A pure JIT model therefore carries more risk for a supermarket than for a factory where production can simply pause.
Secure (3–4): Clear analysis of at least one impact with some development.
Developing (1–2): Identifies an effect without developing reasoning or applying context.
Emerging (0): No valid impact identified.

practice_questions.text: Priya runs a small mail-order skincare business. She is choosing between two suppliers: Supplier A is 10% cheaper but has missed two deliveries in the past year; Supplier B is 10% more expensive but has a perfect delivery record. Justify which supplier Priya should choose.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9): A clear decision with two developed reasons weighed against the alternative, applied to Priya’s context. E.g. Priya should choose Supplier B. Her customers rely on mail-order, so a missed delivery directly means empty shelves and refunded orders — damaging her reputation in a way the 10% saving cannot recover. Reliability protects revenue and customer loyalty; Supplier A’s cheaper price is a false economy because every missed delivery cancels several weeks of savings. The 10% extra from Supplier B is best seen as an insurance premium.
Secure (5–7): A clear judgement with two reasons but uneven development, or limited handling of the alternative.
Developing (3–4): Reasons on both sides but no committed judgement.
Emerging (1–2): Describes the options without choosing.
Around four minutes of the answer should focus on the evaluative judgement.

before.content_html:
What Do Customers Expect?

Quality is not the same thing as ‘expensive’. A Greggs sausage roll and a John Lewis television both have a claim to be ‘quality products’ — but they deliver on very different customer expectations. The sausage roll has to be hot, fresh and consistent every time. The television has to be reliable, cleanly designed and backed by real after-sales support.

Customer expectations cover both the product itself (does it work, does it last, does it match the description?) and the service around it (was staff knowledge good, was delivery on time, if it broke was a refund easy?). Businesses lose customers when the reality falls below what was promised.

Key Fact

Quality has two sides: production of goods (durability, accuracy to specification, zero defects) and provision of services (staff expertise, punctuality, how complaints are handled). A business must manage both.

Consequences of Quality Issues

When quality fails, the consequences stack up fast. Customers return faulty items or demand refunds. Complaints spread on social media within hours. Worst-case, the business has to recall products that are already with customers. Volkswagen’s 2015 emissions scandal forced recalls of millions of vehicles worldwide, cost the company billions in fines, and took years to repair its reputation.

Quality issues do not just affect one-off orders. They trigger fewer repeat purchases, weaker brand image and falling market share, so the real cost is much bigger than the refund bill. Businesses therefore have to identify quality problems before they reach the customer.

How Do Businesses Measure Quality?

Businesses measure quality in several ways: on-the-line inspections, random sampling, customer complaint rates, return rates, online review scores and mystery-shopper reports. A Greggs store manager uses temperature checks and use-by times on food; John Lewis uses satisfaction surveys and net promoter scores to track the service experience.

Problems appear as defects on the production line, rejected goods at the customer end, complaints on review sites, or negative trends in survey data. The classic split is between inspection (checking finished goods and rejecting any that fail) and prevention (designing the process so defects never happen in the first place). Inspection finds problems after they have happened, which means someone has already wasted materials, time and money. Prevention is cheaper but requires more up-front effort.

This insight — that prevention is cheaper than inspection — is what drives Total Quality Management.

Total Quality Management (TQM)

Total quality management (TQM) makes quality everyone’s job. Instead of a separate inspection team catching faults at the end of the line, every worker is trained and empowered to spot problems at their own stage. If something looks wrong, it is fixed there and then.

The advantages are big. Defects are caught early — before expensive later work is added on top. Customer complaints fall, staff feel more engaged because they take ownership, and the brand gains a reputation for consistency. John Lewis built its ‘Never Knowingly Undersold’ reputation on exactly this principle — every partner (employee) sees quality as part of their role.

Key Fact

TQM shifts the focus from inspecting quality in to building quality in. Every employee is trained, empowered and responsible for catching defects at their own stage, not just the inspection team at the end.

Quality Issues When Businesses Grow

Maintaining quality becomes harder as a business grows. Outsourcing means a different company is making part of the product, with its own standards and culture. Franchising spreads the brand to independent local operators whose behaviour is harder for head office to control. McDonald’s, one of the world’s biggest franchises, invests heavily in training and secret-shopper audits to keep quality consistent from Manchester to Miami.

Costs and Benefits of Maintaining Quality

Quality is not free. Businesses face real costs: staff training, inspection equipment, tighter processes, and — when things still go wrong — product recalls. But the benefits are equally real: a strong image and reputation, additional sales, and the ability to charge a higher price because customers trust what they are buying.

The costs fall into four buckets: staff training (building skills so workers spot issues early), inspection costs (labour, equipment, time on the line), product recalls when things slip through, and the one-off hit of bad publicity. The benefits are a better image and reputation, additional sales (new customers and repeat buyers), and a higher price people are willing to pay.

Toyota’s Prius recalls in 2009–2010, covering around 8 million cars worldwide, cost the company an estimated $2 billion — a sobering reminder of what skimping on quality can cost. By contrast, John Lewis has built a generational reputation for service that lets it charge more than discount retailers selling similar goods.

The Big Picture

Quality sits at the intersection of operations, marketing and finance. Get it right and the business earns higher prices, loyal customers and a reputation that competitors struggle to dent. Get it wrong and the refunds, recalls and lost trust can take years to recover from.

before.content_html:
What Is Customer Service?

Customer service is the sum of every interaction a buyer has with a business — from the moment they walk in, call up or click ‘add to basket’ to long after delivery. Good service turns a one-off buyer into a loyal customer. Poor service loses that customer and, increasingly, broadcasts the complaint to thousands of others online.

For this specification you need to understand three methods of good service — product knowledge, customer engagement and post-sales services — plus the benefits, the dangers of getting it wrong, and how ICT has transformed the whole area.

Key Fact

Three methods of good customer service: product knowledge (staff can answer questions accurately), customer engagement (creating a positive experience) and post-sales services (help lines, user training, servicing after the sale).

Product Knowledge

Staff who really understand what they sell save the customer time and build trust. An Apple Store ‘Genius’ guiding a first-time buyer through an iPad, a John Lewis partner comparing two washing machines, a bike-shop mechanic explaining gear ratios — all these turn an uncertain shopper into a confident one. This is also the sales process in practice: attention, interest, desire, action.

Poor product knowledge leaves customers feeling dismissed or misled. Worse, it produces the wrong sale — the buyer returns the item, loses trust, and tells other people.

Customer Engagement

Customer engagement is about the whole experience: the welcome when you walk into a Pret coffee shop, the personalised ‘thanks for your order’ email, the store layout that makes finding items easy, the quick hello on social media when someone tags you in a post. Strong engagement makes customers feel valued and remembered.

John Lewis staff are ‘partners’ — part-owners of the business — and the firm invests heavily in their training. The pay-off is a service reputation that attracts customers prepared to pay more than they would at a discount retailer. The Guide Dogs charity used a similar engagement philosophy when designing their shops, training volunteers to have the longer conversations supporters expect from a charity.

Contrast that with a budget supermarket where staff are deliberately kept to a minimum to keep prices low. Engagement is low by design — but the business is not competing on experience, it is competing on price.

Post-Sales Services

The sale is not the finish line. Post-sales services include help lines when something goes wrong, user training for more complex products, servicing (a boiler check, a car MOT), and easy returns or warranty claims. Currys and John Lewis compete partly on the strength of their after-sales cover — a five-year guarantee included at no extra cost is a decision influence for a big-ticket purchase.

Benefits of Good Customer Service

Good service feeds profit through four linked benefits. Customer satisfaction rises — the buyer feels listened to and valued. This breeds customer loyalty, meaning repeat business that costs far less to win than a new customer. Loyal customers buy more often and try new products, driving increased spend. The end result is higher profitability even though service itself costs money to deliver.

Key Fact

The benefits chain: satisfaction → loyalty → increased spend → profitability. Each step depends on the one before — skip the first and the rest break down.

Dangers of Poor Customer Service

The dangers mirror the benefits — in reverse. Customers become dissatisfied. They tell others, spreading a poor reputation by word of mouth (now mostly amplified online). Sales fall and revenue drops. The damage is not symmetrical: a single bad review can outweigh five good ones, and word of mouth is nearly impossible to control once it gathers speed.

Three ICT developments dominate the specification. Websites give customers 24/7 access to product information, FAQs and self-service — a person can track a parcel at 2am without speaking to anyone. E-commerce extends customer service into the ordering process itself: easy checkouts, saved addresses, one-click returns (ASOS built its reputation on free returns), and personalised recommendations. Social media lets customers reach a brand directly and publicly — a complaint tweeted at a major airline is typically answered within minutes because thousands of others are watching.

The flip side is that failures are also public. A rude response on Twitter or X can be screenshotted and shared thousands of times. Tesco’s ‘out-of-stock tweet’ replies during the 2021 supply squeeze are a textbook example of both the risks and the skill needed to handle social service well.

Why It Matters

Customer service is no longer a department — it is a way of competing. In markets where products are near-identical (banking apps, broadband, supermarkets) service is often the deciding factor. Businesses that invest in product knowledge, engagement and strong after-sales care earn loyalty that pays off year after year; those that cut corners on service usually end up cutting prices too, and still losing customers.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the best example of a post-sales service?
A) An advert on Instagram promoting a new product
B) A store layout designed to feel welcoming
C) A five-year warranty and a help line for troubleshooting a new washing machine
D) A shop mannequin dressed in the latest range
practice_questions.marks: C) A five-year warranty and a help line for troubleshooting a new washing machine [1 mark]

Mastering (2): The tendency of a customer to continue buying from the same business repeatedly rather than switching to a competitor, usually built on trust, satisfaction and positive past experience.
Secure (1): Customers returning to buy from the same business.
Emerging (0): Vague or incorrect — e.g. ‘when a business has lots of customers’.

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit to John Lewis of training its partners to have strong product knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): A clear benefit with a developed chain — e.g. Strong product knowledge lets partners match shoppers to the right appliance (1), which means customers leave satisfied and are more likely to return rather than switch to a cheaper rival (2), lifting repeat revenue and supporting the price premium John Lewis charges (3).
Secure (2): Benefit stated with some development.
Developing (1): Benefit identified without explanation.
Emerging (0): No valid benefit.

practice_questions.text: Last year a retailer had 20,000 customer orders; 14,400 customers returned to place a further order. Calculate the customer-retention rate as a percentage.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): Retention rate = (14,400 ÷ 20,000) × 100 (1) = 72% (2). Correct answer with percentage sign and working (3).
Secure (2): Correct method but arithmetic slip or missing percentage sign.
Developing (1): Ratio 14,400/20,000 shown without converting.
Emerging (0): No valid method. Method marks are awarded even if the final figure is wrong, so working must be shown.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a broadband provider of social-media complaints from dissatisfied customers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): A developed chain of reasoning drawing on more than one factor. E.g. Complaints on X or Facebook are seen by thousands of potential customers, so poor service damages reputation far beyond the individual case. This pushes switchers to rivals when contracts expire, reducing revenue. However, social media also gives the provider a chance to respond publicly — a fast, helpful reply in the same thread can turn the complaint into a marketing moment. The net impact depends on how quickly and skilfully the provider handles the thread; mishandling amplifies the damage, good handling can actually build trust.
Secure (3–4): Clear analysis of at least one impact with some development.
Developing (1–2): Identifies effects without developing reasoning.
Emerging (0): No valid impact.

practice_questions.text: Marcus runs a small electronics shop and is deciding whether to invest £4,000 in a staff-training programme focused on product knowledge and after-sales support. Justify whether he should make this investment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9): A clear decision supported by two developed reasons weighed against the alternative, applied to Marcus’s context. E.g. Marcus should invest. Electronics customers are often uncertain about which product to buy, so trained staff translate that uncertainty into a sale and into confidence that after-sales help will be available if needed. Repeat custom and word-of-mouth are worth far more than £4,000 over a year, especially in a small shop that cannot compete on price with national chains. The alternative — not training — saves the fee but risks losing customers to better-informed rivals, a much bigger long-run cost.
Secure (5–7): A clear judgement with two reasons but uneven development or limited handling of the alternative.
Developing (3–4): Reasons listed each side without a committed judgement.
Emerging (1–2): Describes the options without choosing.
Around four minutes of the answer should focus on the evaluative judgement.
